blocks.text: In the Jensen Huang Saga, Legacy Media Has Officially Lost the Plot

blocks.text: 2 min read

blocks.text: Just when everyone thought the Jensen Huang drama had finally run its course, another plot twist dropped last night.

inlines.text: Just when everyone thought the Jensen Huang drama had finally run its course, another plot twist dropped last night.

blocks.text: The former Nvidia chief posted a long, emotional message pouring his heart out to the public. Right at the end, just as readers figured this was his final goodbye, Huang dropped a stunner: “If the board determines that my return serves the best interests of our shareholders, our employees, our company, and the United States, I would be deeply honored to answer those calls and return as chief executive officer.”

blocks.text: Wait. Could there actually be a comeback? Honestly, looking at how fast the narrative is falling apart, don’t rule it out.

inlines.text: Wait. Could there actually be a comeback? Honestly, looking at how fast the narrative is falling apart, don’t rule it out.

blocks.text: Yesterday, the U.S. Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice (DOJ) put out a joint statement addressing Megaspeed, the company at the center of the AI chip transshipment rumors.

inlines.text: Yesterday, the U.S. Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice (DOJ) put out a joint statement addressing Megaspeed, the company at the center of the AI chip transshipment rumors.

blocks.text: The statement opened with a blunt confession. Normally, the Commerce Department and the DOJ keep their mouths shut when an investigation is still ongoing. This time, though, they had no choice. The circus had gotten so out of hand that both agencies had to break protocol “to provide facts to the public and correct inaccurate information circulating in public reporting.”

blocks.text: So what is this “inaccurate information” floating around in the press?

inlines.text: So what is this “inaccurate information” floating around in the press?

blocks.text: Obviously, it is the blockbuster storyline pushed wall-to-wall by Western mainstream outlets led by The New York Times: that Beijing sent a female spy to seduce Jensen Huang in a classic honeytrap, infiltrated Silicon Valley and the White House, and successfully walked away with restricted U.S. AI chips.

inlines.text: Obviously, it is the blockbuster storyline pushed wall-to-wall by Western mainstream outlets led by

blocks.text: In their joint statement, federal officials talked about Megaspeed and mentioned its CEO, Alice Huang, once. Yet after all that, they reached no conclusion that any illegal chip sales had occurred, and they didn’t put Megaspeed on the U.S. Entity List. In fact, Nvidia itself had proactively cut off Megaspeed a full year ago.

blocks.text: And here is the kicker: not a single word in the entire document mentioned spies or espionage.

blocks.text: In fact, long before and right after Huang stepped down, every official body remotely connected to this story was already busy knocking down the spy rumors.

inlines.text: In fact, long before and right after Huang stepped down, every official body remotely connected to this story was already busy knocking down the spy rumors.

blocks.text: China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Chinese Embassy in the U.S. repeatedly called the espionage claims pure fabrication. Meanwhile, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) published a marathon statement walking through its own investigation into Alice Huang, stating flatly that authorities had “never investigated her for espionage.”

blocks.text: Even on the question of flipping restricted AI chips, Singaporean investigators found nothing to back up the claims.

inlines.text: Even on the question of flipping restricted AI chips, Singaporean investigators found nothing to back up the claims.

blocks.text: Better yet, Singapore threw in some barely disguised shade at Washington. According to the MHA, Singaporean authorities reached out to both the U.S. DOJ and the FBI while looking into the matter, and the Americans completely ghosted them. Then, out of nowhere, U.S. media started blasting out a pile of unverified spy stories. Make that make sense.

blocks.text: Back in Washington, top U.S. officials were saying the exact same thing. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told a press conference that authorities had “never concluded she was a spy.” By November 16, President Donald Trump was also telling reporters that nobody had proven she was a spy.
